title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Host of Ascension (Updated August 31, 2026)
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Host of Ascension Detachment for Genestealer Cults.

The Host of Ascension is more or less the "default" Detachment option for Genestealer Cults, acting as an update of the army's Index Detachment from the start of tenth edition and giving them a powerful buff whenever they arrive from the table as Reinforcements. The rules in this Detachment play very well with the army's ability to put units back into reserves and bring back dead units while giving the army a powerful way to ambush opponents and punch up big into enemy units.

Changelog

  • Update (Current): 2026-08-31 Updated for 11th Edition.
  • Update: 2025-12-11 Updated for Q3 2025 Balance Dataslate.
  • Published: 2025-09-17

Detachment Cost: 3 DP

Force Disposition: Take and Hold

Host being GSC’s only 3 point Detachment at time of launch makes sense but is a bit unfortunate, as the Detachment does take some hits with the rules change that makes them unable to arrive from reserves on turn 1 if you go second. Take and Hold also does seem a bit awkward, not entirely for the fact that your toughness 3 Neophyte Hybrids are generally holding points, but also because in most Take and Hold missions your opponent is rewarded for killing units and this army and Detachment tend to play a lot of chaff. However this is still a Detachment whose lists have a lot of high OC bodies and the strongest toolkit in the army so while it might not be the best choice out the gate, specialists can still make it shine.

Detachment Rule: A Perfect Ambush

Each time a Genestealer Cults unit form your army is set up on the battlefield as Reinforcements, until the end of your next Fight phase, their weapons gain [SUSTAINED HITS 1] and [IGNORES COVER]. 

This is a powerful buff - those are both relevant abilities, with Sustained Hits 1 acting similar to +1 to hit in terms of output and Ignores Cover ensuring that you get the most out of your shooting. The length it lasts is also key - the buffs last into your following fight phase, which both means that they work as a melee buff, but also if you Rapid Ingress or arrive using an Ambush Token, they'll keep those buffs through the shooting phase of the following turn.

Primus. Credit: Rockfish

Enhancements

There are some solid picks here but your go-to is going to be A Chink In Their Armour on a Primus, where the [LETHAL HITS] buff is huge for Neophytes.

  • Prowling Agitant (15pts) – Once per turn, when an enemy unit ends a Normal, Advance, or Fall Back move within 9" of the bearer's unit, if the bearer's unit isn't in Engagement range of an enemy, they can make a reactive Normal move of up to D6". This has some good conditional utility for either gumming up your opponent with units moving closer to their units and controlling movement, or for getting your less durable assets back to safety. You can use this with transports quite effectively to set up re-embarkation traps near objectives or choke points, or with the faction's many Lone Operatives to get multiple uses out of them.
  • A Chink in Their Armour (20pts) – Each time the bearer's unit is set up as Reinforcements, then until the end of your next Fight phase, ranged weapons in the unit have the [LETHAL HITS] ability. A simple ranged damage output buff that's equally at home on a large unit of Neophyte Hybrids or Acolytes with Hand Flamers equipped with Demolition Charges - if you want something gone, this and the Primed and Readied stratagem can put effective damage on anything in the game. Note that unlike the detachment rule this is ranged only; but it does keep the "until your next fight phase" clause - look for opportunities to double up on this with Rapid Ingress into Overwatch. A near auto include.
  • Our Time is Nigh (20pts) – Once per battle, when the bearer's unit declares a charge, you can use this to get +2 to their rolls. Turning a 9" deep strike charge into a 7" charge is enough to more than half the chance you fail, assuming you're willing to sink a command point, and it's also not bad for a Hail Mary on board charges from a rapid ingress to hit additional targets or get some additional utility. Worth including if you have the points
  • Assassination Edict (15pts) – When a model in the bearer's unit makes an attack targeting a CHARACTER unit, they get +1 to hit. This does nothing for a Primus but can be cute if you're taking something like a Benefictus where it helps the character itself hit on 2s. It's particularly useful when you're going up against knights, where the TITANIC knights are also characters.
Genestealers. Credit: Pendulin

Stratagems

These are some expensive Stratagems, with two clocking in at 2 CP after the most recent update.

  • Coordinated Trap (Battle Tactic, 2 CP) – Used at the start of your Shooting phase or the Fight phase on two GSC units that have shot or fought yet. You pick an enemy unit (if it's the fight phase, this unit has to be within Engagement range of both units), and for the rest of the phase, those units get +1 to wound that target. Achilles Ridgerunners and Acolyte Hybrids with Hand Flamers make it almost trivial to have a second unit to activate this with, and it has strong synergy with the wound rerolls or volume of Sustained hits this detachment can kick out.
  • Primed and Readied (Battle Tactic, 2 CP) – Used in your Shooting phase or the Fight phase. Pick a GSC unit that hasn't shot or fought yet and they score Critical Hits on a 5+ instead of 6+. This detachment wants you to play the critical hits lottery and this stratagem is part of the lifeblood of that approach. At 2CP it's extremely pricy, but when you need something to go away with Sustained Hits 1, Lethal Hits, and 20 Models; anything can happen.
  • Tunnel Crawlers (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Movement phase on a unit arriving using the Deep Strike ability. That unit can be set up anywhere more than 6" horizontally from all enemy units, and it's no longer eligible to declare a charge. A perennial nightmare for your opponent's ability to screen their deployment zone and a constant threat to their objectives and staging units: many layouts require your opponent to be exposed to fully cover 6" of an objective, allowing the canny Genestealer Cult player to force their opponent to lose important pieces and take damage just at the threat of this stratagem, without ever needing to use it. Always worth keeping in mind, whether it's for a clutch secondary, primary steal, or just getting some extra guns into rapid fire range.
  • Lying in Wait (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Opponent's Movement phase on one of your BATTLELINE units in Cult Ambush. Until the end of the phase you can set your unit up anywhere on the battlefield within 6" of one of your Ambush Markers and not in engagement range. This is one of the changes from the Q3 update that creates a lot of possibilities while also being very strange to actually use. The requirement to have an Ambush Marker pre-positioned and also have an enemy unit near it, while also not having that unit remove the marker by moving within 9", and being comfortable with how danger close this can put you, is a lot of hoops to jump through. Careful measuring of your opponent's movement ranges (or moving the token with a Nexos or Acolyte Iconward) may be required to get any value out of this stratagem; though there's always the psychological impact of putting an Ambush token somewhere your opponent could get to, while costing them a resource for a purely theoretical play.
  • Return to the Shadows (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Return a Genestealer Cult Infantry unit that is not in engagement range to Strategic Reserves at the end of your opponent's fight phase. Another casualty of the Q3 Dataslate, this is now a generic return to reserve stratagem. Thankfully that's incredibly good here! With the ability to naturally retrigger the A Perfect Ambush detachment rule, as well as A Chink in Their Armour this creates a reliable and repeatable way to maximise your biggest damage units in Host of Ascension, while also offering all the usual scoring efficiency typical of this stratagem archetype
  • A Deadly Snare (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your opponent's Charge phase after they declare a charge against one of your INFANTRY units. Roll a D6; on a 2-4 that enemy unit takes D3 mortal wounds. On a 5+ they take three mortal wounds instead. Sometimes you just need to take the edge off of something - whether it's a big unit that might have the damage to kill your unit otherwise, or something limping along from last turn - being able to reasonably reliably put the hurt on your opponent out of phase is never a bad option to have. You can almost read this as anything with 2 wounds remaining can't charge you, if you squint a little. With the ability to regenerate models from Cult Icons, Genestealer Cults loves its units to cling to life and if this lets you do that, it's worth every command point you spend.

Reductus Saboteur. Credit: Rockfish

Playing This Detachment

Host of Ascension has gone through a wild ride this edition, and broadly has landed in the "mixed arms Jack-of-All-Trades" position within the Genestealer Cult pantheon. Core gameplay loops will generally involve setting up for an overwhelming drop turn where you aim to cripple your opponent's major scoring and damage units, while setting up to minimize the interaction you take back, then using Return to the Shadows and your Resurgence Points to do it all again.

As a result of being a primarily reserves-based army, it's very tempting to go all in on that mechanic. Certainly there's lots of power to be found in leaning into the Neophyte Hybrids + Damage Character (Typically Benefictus or Primus with A Chink in Their Armour), however no longer being able to use this turn 1 with the new changes to the core rules means we do need to invest into being a bit more defensive early on. A core melee piece that can take advantage of Our Time is Nigh to set up clean heroic charges can be enough of a threat that your opponent thinks twice before just throwing their entire army at you. Units that the Biophagus or Benefictus can attach to allow you to still get access to strong stratagem buffs like crit 5s even when you don’t set up from reserves so they can allow you to have a bigger tabletop investment and thusly a sizeable counterpunch.

While Host does like to end the game early with an extremely hard drop turn, they are still more than fine playing out a slow game of attrition utilizing Return to the Shadows to let them easily pick off flanks while a strong core of units holds their center for their Take and Hold disposition. This is an army that can sprint but is also more than comfortable going for a long jog, and which ever one you choose can help guide you on the list you want to take.

Strengths

  • Damage output. Sustained Hits and Ignores Cover are a baseline incredible set of rules for shooting units - the second you add in any of the myriad additional buffs from Characters, Ridgerunners or Stratagems; any unit in the game is under threat from the chosen source of damage.
  • Mobility. With access to multiple ways to get in closer to 9" and great tools for moving units around the board - Resurgence Points and Return to the Shadows, Host of Ascension can move its power around the board and spike its damage or scoring appropriately for many given situations.
  • Versatility. Kill your opponent's primary, kill your opponents units or just good old fashioned jail them in their deployment zone. Do it in shooting, do it in melee or do it with 150 bodies. Host of Ascension will let you play the game you want to.

Weaknesses

  • Inconsistency. If there's any Detachment in the game that likes to ride the lightning, Host of Ascension is it. Whether you're making charges, shooting BS5+ weapons that must do damage, or clinging to life with that last Cult Icon to desperately regenerate onto primary, Host of Ascension will let you fray every nerve in your body. The crushing lows of failing a Benefictus Hazardous check (your character has 3 wounds) to the incredible highs of the natural Box Cars Sustained-Lethal Mining Laser that one shots a target that must die. Host of Ascension lives and dies on you managing the careful risk-reward between trying for too much and failing, and not giving yourself enough chances for variance to smooth out.
  • Vulnerable to Pressure. There's no Fall Back and Shoot here - you're going to be relying on gimmicks like removing casualties to coherency after taking some chip damage, or just plain old keep away to make sure you're firing these T3 5+ save models firing. That goes double for any unit you'd like to Return to the Shadows. 
  • Durability. Everything you can run is made of wet tissue paper with few exceptions: expect things in the open to die and consider it a nice bonus when they don't! At least Resurgence Points are here to make you feel a little better about the unit going down.
  • CP Hungry. This is a Detachment with multiple useable 2CP stratagems, and a natural play pattern that can include spending Return to the Shadows and Primed and Ready repeatedly on your big damage combo - as well as all the incredible situational stratagems like a clutch Go to Ground to have that last Neophyte cling to primary and resurrect 6 friends or every other useable flex stratagem. Expect to want to use Grenade on cool down too - most of your army is carrying the keyword. What this means for list building is scrimping every CP generation unit in the army together - Acolytes with Autopistols to hold your Deployment Zone objective, Reductus Saboteurs to Grenade and potentially even a Nexos to reduce the burden.
Wyrmblade Kill Team. Credit: Rockfish

A Sample List

Hi Floof Cox here, while the old Swarmhost list from last edition was perfection incarnate, here’s an updated style to Host that you might find worth taking a look at. It wants to synergize the damage Neos can do while relying on a brick of Aberrants to help protect any units you place on the center terrain pieces. It’s still got its bag of tricks but with a focus on more damage this time around.

Final Thoughts

Host of Ascension remains an incredibly diverse and interesting Detachment in 11th Edition that is sadly missing a lot of the tools that its former self maintained that made it much better at punishing mistakes. For all that, it maintains an insane level of damage output if you can bring it all to bear, while also having a wonderful amount of redundancy through unit regeneration and high levels of OC, meaning even the failure cases still work if you can hit some charges at the right times. title: Hobby Build Academy: How to Take Better Pictures With a Lightbox
content:
Welcome back Hobby Build Academy students! Once again I am your professor, Marcy, and I'm joined by my amazing assistant, Elly! We've really been enjoying our journey through hobby model building, and we hope you have to; we've really appreciated the comments and feedback we've seen, and we'd love to see if you have been building any models while you read along! This week, we're going to talk a bit about taking better pictures of your models, big or small, by using a lightbox! Now, I know, I know, you might find that scary or complicated, but I promise you that a small investment in a lightbox can make your models look amazing when you photograph them, and also a few things you can consider picking up to make them even better.

Why, though? Well, because taking pictures of your models and figures is half the fun of building them! While it can be great to build, paint, and display them, the era of modern photography at your fingertips means that you can take very good photos with just your phone's default settings, but in most cases, we don't always have access to great lighting, uncluttered backgrounds, and good spaces to take indoor photography of our models. The first step is going to be getting a lightbox, and while we talked about assembling a hobby tool kit a few weeks ago, I wanted to take some special time out to discuss lightbox options, as they can be a little confusing if it is something that hasn't crossed your radar before.

They aren't extravagant, but they get the job done.

Elly: You picked that one up back years ago, do they even make it anymore?

Marcy: I haven't really been able to find it, but there ARE a lot of lightboxes out there; I think a big thing people can get hung up on is what they do and how expensive they seem to be; mine was pretty inexpensive and does everything I'd want it to do, and that really should be the measure for others. In fact, while looking for some to mention in this article, I noticed that one of the most popular on Amazon just looks exactly like the one I use with a different name on it; they really aren't that complicated, although you can obviously invest more if you want.

Look how majestic it is on that thing.

Elly: Basically it needs to have some walls, a light strip, and the ability to hold backings, right? Because I know we saw some that are extremely expensive yet seemed to do the same thing yours does...

Kaito Kid can steal your heart, or the show; it takes very little effort to make things look good in a light box!

Marcy: Yeah; and at our local photography store they do have some VERY nice ones that are quite deluxe, but realistically if you're just looking to take photographs of Gunpla, model kits, miniatures, etc., you can get a lot of mileage out of these inexpensive 10~20 USD kits.

How to Use Your Light Box Effectively

One of the first mistakes I've seen people make with Light Boxes is assuming that they will simply just make everything look better; that isn't really the case, but they can work a lot of magic under the right circumstances. The biggest thing that you'll want to consider out of the box is the use of backings to help give your light box some contrast. Mine came with a few different shades, Black, White, Gray, and you can often find more of these at photography and hobby stores; you can also get creative too with your own ideas for backdrops, but most kits will come with some in the box for you to use.

Even a simplistic model like this can highlight the effect of lighting and shadow in your photos, making it look more dynamic.

Elly: Something really important to remember about photography is that light and shadow play a big role in how your photographs look, and that while the Black backdrop might seem like the most obvious choice, it can sometimes not help depending on what you're trying to photograph. You should probably look for contrasts in your backdrops; for example, a model that is very dark might struggle to stand out against a black backdrop, but also it really depends on what you want the photograph to evoke. Dark backdrops will heighten your model's interactions with light and shadow itself, while lighter ones can make people focus on the colors or overall model; if you go for more decorative backdrops for your photos, you probably want to be careful that the pattern, colors, or other things you've chosen to put in the back don't completely wash out your subject.

SOPMOD here from Girls' Frontline is a great example of posing and positioning. I left in the unflattering sides of the image to prove also that cropping is something you'll want to do; look below.

Marcy: Also, it really does still matter how you pose the models, where you put them, and the photos you take! For my light box, it has a small strip of fabric that helps stop the lights from washing out the box interior, and depending on the angle of my phone, I can still get some really unflattering angles and washed out looks; if you find that your lights are too bright or too dark, play with the way the light box is set up so you can get something that looks natural and doesn't impact the overall models themselves; you don't really want your models to "glow" or shine, and with model kits, you sometimes have to worry about highly reflective chrome stickers, surfaces, or accent pieces that can give you some nasty glare.

by cropping, the photo looks nicer, less "in a box", and also provides more detail and ability to appreciate the subject!

Elly: Although a light box can solve a lot of issues, the room you're in when you use them can also still play a big role; you should try to avoid having the light sources from the room you're in being able to interfere with the box itself; for example, you probably don't want to position the light box towards a window that is currently receiving heavy sun light, and the interior lights in your house are going to also play a role; this can also be true of low light too! A lot of phone cameras try to "help" you take pictures in low light, which can be useful in your day to day life, but when you're trying to do a studio shoot of your favorite model or figure or miniature, it can really give you a pretty sour result.

Adding a Centerpiece: One Turntable and No Microphone

Marcy: If you are really looking to add something a little fun to your light box that can also help make things centered, dynamic, and also allow you to take some nice 360 shots or even video, a miniature turntable is probably the second thing you can or should consider picking up for a light box. Ironically, this might cost you more than the light box itself, so only consider this if you're really enjoying photo shoots and want to have your models look great or play around with angles and positioning; the Mr. Turntable from Mr. Hobby runs around 30 USD, for example, and here's a secret: if it stops turning or runs out of batteries, you still have a solid, stable surface to display things on. Marcy: Please, my father was Mr. Turntable L. Call me Turn.
Elly: BOOOOO

Elly: I don't even remember when we bought this.

Marcy: Me either! We've had this thing about as long as the two of us have been collecting figures of various types together, so... I guess there's a great testament to investing in your hobby and never feeling like you're wasting money on it!

additional benefit: weight.

Elly: Turntables also have an extra benefit, which is that they can help level the surface of your light box if the backing material you're currently using is curving a little away from the light box, making a surface that your model won't always stand on easily. I know with ours, we've had to sometimes use weight objects to keep it from popping up on some of the backings, and the turntable can make that go away extremely easily.

you can even make stupid gifs, like this.

Marcy: They're simple, fairly affordable, and can give you some access to various fun ways to share your models; you can even do dynamic action poses on a turntable, just make sure the model is level and doesn't wobble as you do so. You may also want to ensure your hands are level, such as by placing your elbows on a surface, so that your pictures and videos of the models rotating don't become blurry or out of focus due to the movement of your own body.

Wrap-Up

A light box isn't a necessity, so if you feel like you can't afford or justify one in your living space, even when folded up, then you shouldn't feel like you're doing something wrong by not having one for your hobby. However, you can even make some 'DIY' ones, sometimes which can be as simple as a held up piece of paper and something to diffuse light with, or redirect light. You can sometimes do this with some cardboard and white paper, but if you have the time and money to invest in something like that, I often suggest just looking into a fairly cheap light box like the one listed above.

My girl Olita is nearly 2 feet tall, so she had to sit to fit in the light box, but even so she can take a great picture easily!

Elly: Also, you should remember to pose, crop, and consider your pictures AFTER you take them. While a light box will do a lot to bring out the magic of whatever it is you photograph, you still need to apply some stylistic approaches and common sense to your pictures! Cropping out the 'box' itself, allowing for negative space or angles, and even rotating images after taking them or color correcting them can make even very simple photographs turn into something that looks "professional".

Marcy: These two girls rarely see eye to eye.
Elly: You're really on something today.

Your average phone camera in the last few years has become as capable as most digital cameras, to the point that unless you are going for a very specific look, or have a lot of professional camera equipment laying around, your phone can do all of the work for you. That said, one last tip: if you have shaky or unsteady hands and are worried about pictures after setting up your box, you can find phone camera tripods and other stands that can help angle and position the phone for you. That might require a little research due to the sizes and differences in phones, but you can absolutely find something that can help you take better pictures.

Olita and Agnes can even sit together, but it does show that the bigger the object, the more likely you are to have to 'show' the light box.

Hopefully this little set of tips and suggestions gets you on your own path to enjoying your hobby beyond building it! Models are meant to be displayed, played with, photographed, and customized as you see fit, so there's really nothing wrong with spending a little to get something utilitarian like a light box to go the extra step. title: Contemptor Kevin's Combat Patrol Issue 64 Review
content:
We return in Combat Patrol #64 to the Genestealer Cults and their main battleline unit for the 9th/10th edition Combat Patrol, the Neophyte Hybrids. This is the first issue for the Hybrids. We also more narrative materials and some gaming materials. Does this make the issue worth it? Let's find out.

As always, thank you to Tabletop Battles and Hachette Partworks for the opportunity to review these models, magazines, and materials.

Hobby Materials

This issue gives us one of the two sprues for the Neophyte Hybrids. This sprue has enough parts to build five of the 10 hybrids the unit has, and this Combat Patrol has two units of 10 hybrids. That is a lot of bodies! Most of the minis are 6 pieces, while the special weapons minis are more. That's not quite as good as the Orks or Tyranids, who managed to get their 20 body units down to about 4 pieces in total. But as an older kit, it's still pretty good. These instructions have us build a Cult Icon, Seismic Cannon, Webber, and Heavy Stubber Hybrids alongside 6 carrying regular guns.

Neophyte Hybrids. Credit: Rockfish

The other portion of this issues' hobby materials is an update to "How to Paint our Models" for the Orks and Chaos Space Marines. The issue takes us through relayering the tabards of the Heretics with Warhammer Paint Mephiston Red and highlighting up to Wild Rider Red. We also get our first tutorial for painting Cadian armor, which has us basecoat any trophy rack helmets with Warhammer Paint Caliban Green, and highlighted with Orruk Flesh. The Orks likewise get additional coats of red paint, this time for their eyes. We are also told to highlight any of the red armor plates with Wild Rider Red. We also, somewhat curiously to my eyes, get told to highlight the Ork skin with Wraithbone. That strikes me as a more stark highlight jump than I would be comfortable with.

Ork skin done. Credit: Rich Nutter

Narrative Materials

Our first narrative section is Part 15 of Bonds of Honour. When we last left Squad Askarton of the Silver Templars, the Kin of the Leagues of Votann had convinced this Intercessor Squad to fight a green tide of Orks and slay the Warboss. And the Warboss was big and bad. "He was a colossal beast, with more neck than head and teeth that you could have stuck in the ground and used as a fortification." The Intercessors shredded many an Ork with their Bolt Rifles, but because there were so many Orks they were able to get in for close quarters combat. The Marines draw their combat knives, and begin stabbing the Orks. However, because there were so many Orks they began to sufficiently dent Marine armor that it was causing wear and tear. Eventually Brother Dharrion failed his saving throw, and took a Choppa to the knee. This break in the Marine line "undid" Squad Askarton, forcing them closer to their wounded Battle Brother but keeping them immobile. Against the green tide, this was death. Squad Askarton was in deep trouble.

"But then, something happened that would completely turn their fortunes around."

The second narrative article is on the "Arsenal of Ascension", which discusses how and where the Genestealer Cults source their armaments. Usually by stealing them, but other times by adapting or manufacturing their own weapons. There are, after all, plenty of Genestealer Cultists in the Departmento Munitorum who ensure that a shipment of Lasguns here, a crate of grenades there goes "missing". The Cultists, oftentimes being heavy industrial engineers, are able to repurpose mining or construction equipment into military weapons. Lastly, many of the biomorphic cultists have their own, alien-grown bioweapons like claws or bone swords.

Gaming Materials

We get the data card for the first Neophyte Hybrid unit. In this iteration of Combat Patrol, they're a T3, 5+ 1 Wound unit with deep strike. There's a lot of them and they can shoot from anywhere, which is their special skill. They die to almost anything that can shoot them though.

The other gaming element in this issue is Campaign: Aeldari vs. Leagues of Votann. The Aeldari are looking for a band of missing Rangers, or at least their spiritstones. Meanwhile, the Kin are trying to find additional resources and run into the Aeldari. They fight in "A Clash of Patrols". As I'm a Marines player, I find myself rooting for the Kin in the eternal Elves vs. Dwarves fight.

Elves vs. Dwarves are a feature in all GW games. Credit: 40khamslam.

We do not get a lot of substantive gaming material in this issue, because we do not have the fully Hybrid Metamorph unit yet.  But that can be next week's fun.

The Final Verdict

Another well-balanced issue of Combat Patrol, with some helpful hobby guides, interesting narrative materials (including the multi-chapter Bonds of Honor), and the time-honored "Elves versus Dwarves" fight. We also get a sprue of a troop unit that can build fully half the unit, which means if you were stuck with two copies of this issue you could still get a full unit of Hybrids. While the gaming materials feel a bit light by comparison to some of the more recent issues, we still have at least something to roll our dice with.  That's a good deal in my book!

Until next time Combat Patrolers!

title: New pre-orders include support for 40k's golden guardians and Old World armies galore
content:
In a refreshingly broad crop, Games Workshop has announced that the new Custodes Support Battle Group is now up for pre-order alongside Battle March armies for five Warhammer: The Old World factions. The Support Battle Group includes an impressive range of new sculpts, ready to provide armored support for your 40k or Horus Heresy Custodes army. While the Battle March Armies do not contain any fresh sculpts of their own, fans of Warhammer Fantasy will likely enjoy the retro fantasy aesthetics on display.

The new Custodes Support Battlegroup takes pride of place at the top of the latest Warhammer Community pre-order post. The set itself contains six models: one Telemon Heavy Dreadnought, one Pallas Grav-attack, and four Gryfalcon Jetbikes. It is worth noting, however, that the set is currently sold out online. As such, you may well have to wait until launch day on September 12 until you're able to get your hands on the set. You may also be able to track down a pre-order in-store at your local Warhammer shop.

That said, Horus Heresy enjoyers can still pre-order the new Journal Tactica: Prospero Burns - The Judgement Of Valdor, which includes plenty of lore and a new army list for Daemons of Tzeench.

I am also pleased to report that online pre-orders for the five upcoming Warhammer: The Old World Battle March armies are still in stock at the time of writing. Five Old World factions are served here: the Empire of Man, the Beastmen Beayherds, the Wood Elf Realms, the High Elf Realms and the Orc and Goblin Tribes.

For those not in the know, Battle March is an agile format for Old World designed to cater to smaller armies at around 750 points. The goal is to provide fast-paced, accessible games with a lower barrier to entry where you don't have to paint hundreds of miniatures to get stuck into a game. Each of the five boxes is designed to provide an army that does just this.

title: SCP Foundation meets Control in this narrative board game Kickstarter
content:
In perhaps one of the most fascinating board game crowdfunders I've ever seen, The Altered: Anomaly Containment Archives has you and up to three other players participate in a narrative-driven game of bureaucratic horror where you have to assess the essential humanity of a group of poor unfortunates. It's creeping, otherworldly horror, reminiscent of foreboding internet sensation the SCP Foundation, critically acclaimed supernatural thriller video game Control, and recent horror blockbuster The Backrooms.

You'll do this by interacting with over 1,000 pages of physical documentation as part of four interconnected cases (seven if you back the Kickstarter campaign at a higher tier). There are also over 40 props, which the developer calls "tactile artefacts," for you to assess as you make your judgements. Though narrative-driven, The Altered doesn't require a GM and isn't, strictly speaking, a TTRPG. Instead, the intrigue and facts of each case are presented to you as you play through the game.

The Kickstarter campaign has already raised an impressive £260,000 ($325,000) and still has 40 days to go.

Set in the techno-dystopian city of New Harbor, the Covenant Life Assurance Company requires you to act as a life insurance assessor for the Biological Asset Risk division. You'll be investigating anomalous cases amongst underwritten clients. Each sigantor you investigate is a human (or former human) who got a little bit too close to an anomaly. Your job is to assess the extent to which they're still human. It looks to be gruelling, high-stakes stuff, and exactly what you'd expect from the best board games of the genre.

One downside of the campaign, however, is the sheer number of stretch goals and additional goodies that you can get your hands on. The exact list is too complex to lay out in detail here, but expect additional maps, commemorative medals, fancy seals, an art book, and stretch goals galore. However, if you can wade through the eldritch complexity of the campaign itself, you'll be rewarded with a look at a fascinating project.

You won't find any eldritch anomalies on the Wargamer Discord - honest!

title: Reality Fracture MTG boosters may be scarce thanks to literal drought, says Wizards
content:
In some disappointing news courtesy of the world's increasingly precarious global shipping lanes, it looks as though booster pack supply for the upcoming Reality Fracture MTG set may be limited at release for players in North America. Wizards of the Coast has reported that a drought in a nearby lake has caused shipping disruptions along the Panama Canal due to a lack of water.

For the uninitiated, the Panama Canal is an artificial waterway that allows ships to transit between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans without having to sail around South America. It shaves a huge amount of time off of shipping voyages and is an instrumental part of the global supply chain. This, it would seem, includes MTG cards.

According to a statement from Wizards, one of the ships caught in the disruptions is carrying a supply of Reality Fracture Play Boosters bound for North America.

"For most stores and players, you're unlikely to notice an issue during Prerelease weekend or even release weekend," said the statement. "However, the supply of Play Boosters may dry up quickly," it continues. "We currently expect a replenishment within a few weeks of the release of Reality Fracture. So, there may be a short period after the set's release where Play Boosters are hard to come by."

Fortunately, according to Wizards, only Play Boosters have been affected by the shipping disruptions, meaning that the other products for the upcoming MTG set will almost certainly be unaffected.

Reality Fracture offers a return to MTG's original setting with an intriguing twist. Set in an alternate reality where the events of MTG's past have been altered, we can expect curious alternate versions of classic characters. Personally, I'm most excited about Hexhaven, a twisted, militaristic shadow of the magical school of Strixhaven.

Reality Fracture will release on October 2.

title: Pokémon TCG Pocket's new Team Rocket update reminds us it's good to be bad
content:
Despite hundreds of hours spent watching Pokémon cartoons as a child urging me to "prepare for trouble," I'm not sure I ever quite managed it. Ever since the Team Rocket Pokémon TCG set first came to the West in April 2000, I'd always been captivated by the darker, meaner, edgier side of Pokémon. A childhood spent watching Ash and pals triumph over Team Rocket spawned in my mind an indelible question: what if the bad guys got a turn? Pokémon TCG Pocket's latest expansion follows this train of thought in a big way, revitalising the sinister feel of the old school Team Rocket cards for the modern age.

The Team Rocket's Ambition expansion has brought plenty of sinister takes on classic Pokémon to the app. All three legendary birds (that's Articuno, Moltres, and Zapdos) have Team Rocket variants. Team Rocket's Articuno is particularly flavorful, boasting an extremely powerful attack which hurts your benched Pokémon in the process - that's some classic Team Rocket cruelty.

There are a few new beefy trainer cards in the game, too. Team Rocket's Theiving Machine lets you take a random item card from your opponent's discard pile, offering a fun and flavorful option. We've also got Team Rocket's Boss, which allows you to force your opponent to play their Basic Pokémon - ideal if you're looking to punish some weak 'mons to get more prizes.

While it's too early to say if these new additions amount to the best Pokémon cards out there, the art on offer is as sumptuous as it is sinister. Team Rocket's Boss in particular oozes with larcenous intent, showing Giovanni with his trademark smirk. Team Rocket's Master Plan also includes a pair of plucky grunts, likely moments before being forced to blast off (again).

If you, like me, enjoy the edger side of retro Pokémon, then the new update may well be exactly what you're looking for.

title: Revolution tastes sweet in DnD rival Daggerheart thanks to this homebrew
content:
Dungeons and Dragons is the perennial rival of every single fantasy TTRPG that comes out. Of those alternatives, Daggerheart has undeniably put a dent in the icon's golden armor. Backed by TTRPG darlings at Critical Role, Daggerheart set its sights for the players who adore the narrative side of the tabletop experience, and it has succeeded at that. And just like any beloved TTRPG should, the homebrew has grown fast.

And as this setting proves, it's far from half-baked.

A Sweet Resistance by Busca takes place in Candora, a land of sugary sweets under the grip of the Insectoid Primacy. Despite the sucralose setting, the warfare here wouldn't be out of place in Warhammer 40k 11th edition. Perhaps not grimdark, but more sourshade? The players may be candy, but the themes of rebellion reign strong in this setting, and that adds a lot to the homebrew's charm. Whoever said whimsy wasn't rebellion clearly isn't familiar with history.

The influences of the saccharine dystopia include Adventure Time, Disco Elyisum and Andor. In line with these games, you fall under deadlier dangers the more  you uncover the insectoid conspiracy.  The Sweetness Level, which one can liken to Grand Theft Auto's "Wanted Level," dictates just how fiercely the authoritarian regime will throw its forces at you.

Naturally, a regime of this magnitude can't be brought down with protests alone. As their pincers bite deeper, you must utilize an arsenal of sugar weapons against them. This is where the Adventure Time influence really shines, with fun candy-themed weaponry and power-ups. As a player, it is your sworn duty to make as many dessert-themed puns as candidly possible. Even the familiar DnD races will have some type of sweet twist,  so watch out for those.

A Sweet Resistance is actually part of a collection titled Tales & Twists, which features other brand-spanking new settings to sink your teeth in. This is an incredible time to be a Daggerheart player. If you love Critical Role's style of TTRPG gaming, then Daggerheart's the game to look out for.

title: Hunter: The Parenting makes me yearn for more World of Darkness adaptations
content:
Among tabletop RPGs, World of Darkness once reigned as the de facto number two behind the iconic dungeon crawling classic. The series quietly built up a cult following so vast that would make upholding the Masquerade a near impossible task.  Yet despite its popularity, the World of Darkness never got as many adaptations as it deserved. Such a deep world has so many stories to tell, and for the longest time, that itch went unscratched.

That is, until the premiere of a now iconic web serial.

Hunter: The Parenting is a web series developed by Ogre Popenang, the team behind Warhammer 40k fan darling "What if the Emperor had a Text to Speech Device?" While it's unfortunate that the series never made it to the Warhammer 40k 11th edition era, it spawned a worthy successor. Hunter: The Parenting follows a bombastic man of an "Imperial" persuasion alongside his massive family of misfits as they hunt down all that stalks in the night.

Though the series' foundations are built upon the pre-existing characters from their 40k forebear, it has undoubtedly created a world all its own. What makes Hunter: The Parenting so good perhaps lies in not being a parody, but an outright story set in the world. The mix of grimdark supernatural horror with clown fiesta urban fantasy showcases a serious love of the material.

I also love how many big swings the series takes with World of Darkness lore. I won't spoil specifics, but needless to say, there's a reason I call this a World of Darkness story. It does not tie itself down to one game. Just as Warhammer 40k factions clash in their personal agendas, so too do the Hunters get caught in supernatural wars they know terrifyingly little about. My personal favorite episode, Chapter 5.2, involves a visit to my home country, the Philippines. Hunter: The Parenting comments on colonization and its effects on local superstition in such a clever and dramatic way, all while paying respect to my culture.

The only bad thing about Hunter: The Parenting is that there isn't nearly enough of it. I sincerely hope Hunter: The Parenting shows White Wolf just how awesome a World of Darkness series can be with great writers and artists at the helm, even in an indie capacity.

title: This charming free Warhammer scenario makes me feel like a kid again
content:
The lone tower on a hill makes for one powerful fantasy trope. In The Lord of the Rings, Saruman plots to overthrow the Free Peoples of Middle-earth from one such tower, while in Dungeons and Dragons these towers can contain anything from brooding necromancers to hordes of treasure. They're mysterious, they're imposing, and they're a storytelling goldmine. This is likely why Games Workshop has released a simple yet irrepressibly charming tower-based scenario for Warhammer: The Old World's agile Battle March format.

The scenario itself pits two armies of up to 750 points against one another in a contest for a mysterious tower in the centre of the battlefield. However, as with any mysterious fantasy tower worth its salt, the building contains a "Disgruntled Occupant" (Games Workshop's words, not mine). To occupy the tower, you'll need to send in a character or a unit with Unit Strength 10 or less.

However, once you attempt to occupy the tower, you'll spawn an occupant from an amusing little table. Trolls, Ogres, and even a Dubious Wizard are all possibilities. Oust the occupant, and you'll have an extra 100 Victory Points for your trouble.

What's most pleasing about this free scenario, however, is how it is utterly laden with fantasy nostalgia. Not only is it centred around a classic piece of Warhammer terrain, but, should you face the Dubious Wizard, you don't even get to fight. Instead, you must solve a riddle by passing a leadership test - just the right kind of silly.

No matter your Old World faction of choice, this scenario offers a light, playful twist on the small-scale Battle March format - ideal for anyone just starting out in Warhammer: The Old World who might be looking for an excuse to indulge in some fantastical nostalgia. I just hope my poor Bretonnian Paladin is up to the task should she come face-to-face with a riddle-spewing maniac.

title: Gothic survival board game to get rerelease and expansion in new crowdfunder
content:
When night settles in and the shadows grow long, horrors and monsters come forth from the yawning darkness, keen to snuff out the candle of civilisation. It's a tried and tested horror trope that survival tower defense board game Aberration aims to bring to the tabletop. The well-received fantasy horror board game is getting another print run and a brand new expansion, Oblivion's Embrace, all thanks to a new crowdfunder.

The crowdfunding project is going well, having reached nearly $150,000 (£111,000) with 18 days left to go. This not only means that the campaign will likely be a safe bet, but it also means you've got plenty of time to decide if the title is right for you.

At its core, Aberration offers a cooperative tower defense experience for one to four players. You'll use asymmetric powers, worker placement mechanics, and bag building elements to defend a village beset by deadly horrors. This is all framed by a gorgeous board and a detailed range of miniatures.

Though I've not played the game myself, Aberration comes from the talented mind of veteran game designer Peter Lee, responsible for the gorgeous worker placement game Lords of Waterdeep (which I hold to be one of the best board games of all time).

There are four pledge levels. Bürach Defender costs $95 (£70) and nets you the core game, while Oblivion's Embrace sets you back $139 (£103) and adds the expansion by the same name to the mix.

Those looking for the other expansion can go for the Aberration Hunter pledge. Coming in at $179 (£132), this one includes the core game, Oblivion's Embrace, and the Arcanists and Abominations expansion. Lastly, we have the aptly named All-In, which comes to a chunky $275 (£203). This includes everything in Aberration Hunter as well as a range of smaller add-ons. Notably, each pledge comes with access to applicable stretch goals, too.

What makes a good survival horror game? Tell us your thoughts on the Wargamer Discord.

title: The latest MTG lore guide has me bathing in unsettling dystopian goodness
content:
Amid my crippling Universes Beyond fatigue, I find myself desperate for a return to Magic: The Gathering's rich original setting. The upcoming MTG set, Reality Fracture, offers an intriguing subversion of Magic's established canon, turning the edifice on its head as part of an effort from hubristic mind-mage Jace Beleren to make his own, sanitised universe. On August 28, Wizards published a juicy lore preview for the set, giving us plenty to chew on ahead of its launch on October 2.

Reality Fracture is something of a departure from MTG sets of the past. Starting off in an effort to escape the trauma of the Phyrexian Invasion and the scars it left on the Multiverse, Jace Beleren started with a thought experiment: what if the universe had simply been better? As Wizards' latest lore article tells us, this didn't go well, and eventually wound up with the worst possible version of Jace creating his own pet dimension: The Echoverse.

While the Echoverse departs from the known MTG Multiverse in a wide variety of ways, the article focuses on Hexhaven Academy, a dark, militaristic mirror to the whimsical magical school of Strixhaven. Here, Jace rules from a great tower on the campus, filled with faceless guards and impossible, twisting corridors.

In the Echoverse, Hexhaven is surrounded by a deadly wasteland populated by mage-eating horrors known as The Eradia. In response to this threat, the five schools of Hexhaven subject their students to rigorous military training to produce battlemages.

Five Schools make up the glorified military academy: the diviners of Fatehold, the knowledge-hungry Theorix, the building-obsessed Konstrari, the invasive healers of Vigorbloom, and the battlepoets of Stingerquill.

To add to the dystopian horror, Jace forces every cadet to wear a badge bearing the likeness of his own eye and deliberately trains the students to make them more susceptible to mind-reading. It's darkly compelling stuff, and I can't wait to see more.

title: Pokémon TCG Pocket is getting a crunchy new card type
content:
Mewtwo be upon ye! In welcome news for fans of the Pokémon TCG's mobile incarnation, The Pokémon Company has announced that Dual-type cards will be coming to the game in October. Revealed at the PokémonXP panel today, the announcement came hand in hand with an adorable new trailer that's well worth a watch if you're even remotely interested in watching adorable pocket monsters engage in wholesome shenanigans.

Front and center is Mega Mewtwo X ex, the poster 'mon for the arrival of Dual-type cards to Pokémon TCG Pocket. However, the video description for the trailer tells us that they're "starting with" the new Mewtwo, meaning that we can almost certainly expect more Dual-type cards down the line.

We're also getting Piplup ex and Fuecoco ex as part of the October update. Though these two adorable starters very much occupy the opposite end of the Pokémon spectrum to Mewtwo, it's edifying to see that ex versions of partner Pokémon will soon arrive on the app.

Dual-type Pokémon were first added to the paper TCG way back in 2003, but it was 2016's XY Steam Siege set that really popularised the mechanic.

For the uninitiated, Dual-type cards may seem a little unintuitive. However, the mechanics surrounding these versatile monsters are actually deceptively simple - a quality shared by many of the best Pokémon cards.

Like single-type Pokémon, these fellows follow the usual rules for type weaknesses. For instance, with Mega Mewtwo X ex, any Dark Type attacks will inflict an additional 20 damage. The difference comes when Dual-types attack. When targeting an opposing Pokémon's weakness, you can use either type on the card. This means that our pal Mewtwo can hit extra hard against 'mons who are weak to Psychic or Fighting-type attacks.

title: New Tabletop Battles App and Administratum Updates: August 29, 2026
content:
Welcome back to more app updates! We talked last time around about adding support for StarCraft in the Tabletop Battles app, plus some additional updates for Kill Team, Warhammer 40k, and Age of Sigmar. This time around we have some more new and exciting updates to share - not just around Tabletop Battles, but also Administratum.

If you haven't downloaded the app yet, you can get it through one of the links below:

Today's update is live on Android and iOS.

Tabletop Battles: The August 2026 Balance Update

We've updated the Tabletop Battles app to include the new layouts for missions in the 2026-27 missions pack, reflecting the layout changes from the latest balance update. We've also updated the Dispositions on a few Detachments which changed, and fixed a few lingering bugs.

As a quick aside, I'd like to take a moment to remind people that you can compare scores to opponents in the Tabletop Battles app using our Game Link feature - this has been around for years, and lets you view your opponent's score in app, and will alert you whenever your scores line up. It's a pretty solid feature that lets you square up whenever you need.

So why don't more people use it? Well the answer is because it's one of the few features which requires you to log into the app, and most people don't. We've always prioritized ease of use and speed with the app - our philosophy is that you should be able to show up at an event, download the app for the first time, and immediately play, no subscription or bullshit required. But that means some more complicated features can get missed. So if you're wondering why Game Link and "generate code" aren't showing up on your create game screen, that's the most likely reason.

Administratum 4.0

We've been hard at work on a new version of Administratum, and the first version of it has finally released. This is a big step for us for two reasons: The first is that we're finally decoupling Administratum from Crusade. This isn't just because Crusade seems to be gone in tenth Edition 40k; it's also because we wanted to open up Administratum to work with other game systems, so you could use it to run Age of Sigmar, Trench Crusade, StarCraft, Necromunda, or anything else.

To activate this version of the app, just click on the handy "V4" button on the upper left. NOTE: Your current rosters and campaigns won't transfer to V4. We're going to leave the old version alive for quite a some time while we build out new features and support in the app, so don't worry too much about losing this old data.

This first version has some cool new features for managing your roster, letting you create templates for common units and set some rules for how much things cost. It's not a full roster builder in that we aren't putting all the unit profiles in there or GW rules, but if enterprising players can certainly treat it as such if they want to put those values in. We've always thought Administratum could use some kind of roster builder, but one built around "what units do I own" and not "what list do I want to make." There will be more work to be done on this.

Of course, we also just support Crusade in the new Administratum, and will be working on updates to that framework as well. We have some plans for what we want to do around Crusade in the platform - stay tuned for those.

If you haven't used Administratum yet, give it a look - it's pretty great, and doesn't need Crusade now.

What's Next?

We're working on a few more features for StarCraft support, plus ongoing development on Administratum and some new Crusade-like things we're supporting. We'll also be updating support for Age of Sigmar to add the new Ogors rules and rules for the Sons of Behemat when those rules release. The work never stops here on our end but if we miss anything, let us know.

Why Use Our App?

We've seen this question pop up once or twice from players who aren't familiar with our app, or whose introduction is the War Journal in the Warhammer 40,000 app. Well, there are a few reasons:

  • Runs faster and better. Tabletop Battles is built in Flutter and not React. Flutter is less common but removes a lot of runtime jank that can bog down React Native apps. If you've noticed that TTBA runs faster, this is a primary reason why. Flutter generally outperforms React Native and uses less CPU and as a result, less battery.
  • Built-in stats screens. If you want more than just a list of your games, we've got you covered, and we're working on more personal stats you can access via our Edge web app.
  • Faction trackers. If you want to track things like Pain tokens or Saga progress, our app has that.
  • Other game modes. Do you want to play asymmetric missions? track custom games? Do you need a different disposition than the one you're allowed to select? The Tabletop Battles interface is much more flexible, and allows for custom score input.
  • Direct feedback. We read every bug report and work to implement changes, and we respond to inquiries on Discord. The Tabletop Battles app is very much what you help make it.

Also it's free - we don't get any money from you using our app. If anything, it costs us money. We're just in it to make the best possible app for tracking games of tabletop wargames.

So if you haven't already, give the app a download and check out our newest features. Everything shown today is available in our apps, right now.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Thoughts

Chris has been kind enough to send us a comprehensive writeup of both his list, and the final game. Let's find out how such an unusual build holds together:

Chris: This list was built to work off of the Disruption missions by keeping primary scores as low as possible, using my mobility to either punish my opponents primary or to press hard to end games early.  The list works in three aspects to best accomplish the goal.  The scoring element of the list uses two squads of chaos cultists to both screen the backfield against opponents and maintain space to deepstrike using Warpstrike Champions defensively if needed. Working in concert, the unit of Red Corsairs as well as the Bestmen are there for early game scoring.  With how popular Take and Hold is as a disposition, it's important to have a setup that can get me 15 primary points turn one if I go first, giving me a huge advantage from the outset. The final element of scoring rests in the solo Terminator Lord, who deepstrikes alongside a Terminator block to trigger free Siegebreaker Strike for Ignore Cover, and provides a late game action piece that can be challenging to remove effectively.

The second aspect of the list is the two main hammer thrusts in the form of the two ten-man Terminator squads with Sorcetors.  Each of these squads are kitted out for maximum firepower with bolters and autocannons.  One of the sorcerers has Ashur’s Binding Runes to further provide a hefty turn one threat.  Just having the threat present in the list of a turn one deepstrike makes opponents play games differently.  The sorcerer also provides some very nice utility to the squads such as access to Death Hex (the ability to grant extra AP to a unit) as well as re-roll charges.  When this combines with the Portal of Spite stratagem it gives the unit a 7” charge re-rolling.  A turn one Deep Strike from tenTterminators shooting and clogging a backfield can be crippling for some armies.  The second terminator squad becomes a turn 2-3 threat to engage in concert with the other combat units to overwhelm the opponent.  Both of the units benefit from the Cabal of Chaos giving the units access to healing, as well as the shooting bonus strength which helps with toughness breakpoints.

The final aspect of the list is the two melee haymakers from the Huron Terminator squad and Kravek's Mulitators.  Each of these has a different role that helps shore up weaknesses in the list.  Huron’s squad swaps autocannons for heavy flamers to help with horde clearance as well as having an overwatch threat to deny opponents secondaries.  Huron’s aura ability can not be understated here either, as in a very elite list such as this an aura of +1 OC is huge when trying to deny primary.  Since, most Disruption missions only require the player to hold a single objective, this allows Huron to deny central objectives against other dispositions who need to hold 2 or more objectives.  Kravek is the best answer to Defilers and knights.  This list has a weakness for mass tough hulls and Kravek gives an answer to at least take out one threat to protect the terminators.

The Final Game: 

In the final game of the event I was facing off against Astra Militarum running Mechanized Assault and Abhuman detail.  Since my opponent had a Stormlord full of Ogryn I had to respect its threat ranges, as with Rapid Fire a squad could (and later in the game did) disembark and  maul an entire terminator squad.  We were playing on layout B and I got the first turn, which is usually a good thing for my army but my opponent deployed very defensively giving me no targetss turn one for aggression. I did get Secure as an easy turn one Secondary, and held and Forward Position.

My opponent also played a very defensive turn one, only sending out five Ratlings to retake the central objective and staged his Bullgryn in offensive positons, after which I returned my 2nd Terminator squad, and Kravek to deepstrike.  On my turn two I drew Beacon and Center Ground.  Seeing my opponent place his Bullgryn so far forward, I decided now was the moment to strike.  Both of my Terminator squads arrived with line of sight on the Bullgryn squads, and both also made the charge, killing one Bullgryn unit outright, and leaving the second squad to just 2 models left.  In the center my Red Corsair Raiders also killed the ratlings, unlocking their improved OC.

On my opponents turn he prepared for the crack back. The Terminator squad on my opponents expansion faced full Ogryn and Scion squads, while the others were assailed by two Scion squads (one of which was led by Yarrick) and the Stormlord.  While my Terminator squad on the objective was reduced to just two models, and the other to just the Sorcerer alone, neither squad died fully, denying my opponent his Secondary and Primary for turn 2.  My opponent made the decision to urgently try to score points, and he charged Yarrick’s squad into my Red Corsair Raiders, I used my -1 AP stratagem and only lost two models, and then killed 6 scions back, allowing the remaining Raiders to hold the objective thanks to being OC3 each.

On my turn three I brought in Huron and Kraveks units and sealed the deal, making a 12” charge onto my opponents home and a 10” charge to destroy his Ogryn squad.  At the end of my turn three my opponent was left with just A stormlord and a smattering of weakened units testing Battle-shock, and that was it.

Thoughts

Bike and Allarus Custodes vs. Ravener-heavy Invasion Fleet here, playing a Take and Hold mirror that's sure to get extremely violent. Asset-wise, the key units on each side feel like the Raveners (obviously, super killy and quite durable with a 5+ Feel No Pain available) and primary-denying Hormagaunts for the Tyranids, and the Wardens and Venatari for the Custodes. The Allarus are fine here, and enjoy getting to do re-rolls against the Raveners, but they're also pretty vulnerable to getting devoured by said snakes. The Wardens are a very different kettle of fish, as the AP reduction from Valerian combines with their once-per-game Feel No Pain to create something that can plausibly face tank a full Ravener brick, then cause some problems in return. The Venatari, meanwhile, will kill pretty much whatever they touch after ingress, and the Tyranids don't have that many alpha units, so have to respect them.

Good tools on both sides, and also some ways to work around them. Maleceptors help with the Warden problem, as if they snipe a few off with D3 shots, the overall threat presented by the unit diminishes considerably. In the other direction, the Allarus into Hormagaunts feels like overkill, but that doesn't stop them turning them into dust the second they so much as look in that direction, and just in general the Custodes enjoy being surprisingly near parity on activations. That said, into Invasion Fleet (with access to the Feel No Pain stratagem), the small Bike units are less useful than they'd normally be, as they won't reliably do enough to justify their price tag. The last big potential curveball here is Shadow - more activations makes the Custodes less likely to suffer a total blowout here, but if they've already lagged behind, it could be a real killing blow.

Who wins, then? I think what probably ends up sealing this here is the free double Ingress the two Ravener units can do. Tyranids winning this game reliably needs both Ravener units to make good charges, but it turns out Ingress > 10" movement makes that pretty comfortable to set up, and I don't think there's quite anything the Custodes can do to stop it. Being aggressive with the bikes (since they won't be that useful otherwise) can maybe delay this somewhat, but I doubt it's enough, and the bugs were triumphant.
